_template_meta.purpose: Canonical reference template for SAFE Framework STIX 2.1 bundles. Covers all object types, all fixes identified in TFA/SAFE audit (March 2026), and forward architecture for TAXII readiness and intelligence pipeline.

terminology.coordinates: SAFE calls what STIX/MITRE calls 'tactics' COORDINATES — because each represents the intersection of three dimensions (mode × mechanism × domain) in the harm taxonomy. The STIX type remains x-mitre-tactic for ecosystem compatibility, but the concept is a SAFE coordinate.
terminology.techniques: Same as MITRE — a specific method of harm. SAFE techniques span direct, proxy, and tech-facilitated vectors.
terminology.vector: SAFE-specific concept. Whether harm is delivered directly (perpetrator→victim), via proxy (perpetrator→third-party→victim), or tech-facilitated (perpetrator→technology→victim). TFA Matrix = the tech_facilitated subset.

extension_id_registry._note: Sequential UUIDs within the NAS namespace. The x-safe-delta.json currently uses ...000000000002 which conflicts with the technique extension — needs updating to ...000000000003.

_template_meta.taxii_readiness: This template includes an x-mitre-collection object which is the handshake for TAXII distribution. A TAXII server advertises collections; consumers poll for updates. Even without a TAXII server, including the collection object means the bundle is ready to be served via TAXII if/when one is stood up. The bundle URL (GitHub raw or site) can be polled directly by platforms as a lightweight alternative.

architecture_decisions.dual_kill_chains: DECIDED: Techniques carry THREE kill chain phases: (1) safe-harm-taxonomy (27 SAFE coordinates - mode.mechanism.domain), (2) tfa-matrix (9 TFA activity-type tactics, for tech_facilitated techniques), (3) safe-harm-lifecycle (9 lifecycle phases, multiple per technique). Each kill chain serves a different purpose and audience. STIX kill_chain_phases is an array - designed for exactly this.
architecture_decisions.coordinates_not_tactics: SAFE calls what STIX/MITRE calls 'tactics' COORDINATES. The STIX type is x-mitre-tactic for ecosystem compatibility. Each coordinate is a mode × mechanism × domain intersection.
architecture_decisions.lifecycle_as_kill_chain: The harm lifecycle is NOT a standalone framework. It's a third kill chain on techniques. Techniques appear across MULTIPLE lifecycle phases (a technique used in 'taking-action' may also be used in 'keeping-a-hold'). This directly feeds case management pattern detection.
architecture_decisions.validation_not_citation: Aggregate validation evidence (source categories, observation counts, confidence) rather than individual case citations. Protects survivor privacy. Only populated when data is meaningful.
architecture_decisions.cross_framework_extensibility: Additional frameworks (DISARM, MITRE ATT&CK, grooming lifecycle, etc.) can be added as additional kill chain phases on the same technique object. One object, many views, no duplication.

safe-harm-taxonomy.description: SAFE coordinates - mode × mechanism × domain intersections. The analytical backbone.

tfa-matrix.description: TFA activity-type tactics. The communication layer for the public TFA website.

safe-harm-lifecycle.description: Lifecycle phases - when in the attack sequence does this technique appear. Techniques can appear across MULTIPLE phases.
safe-harm-lifecycle.audience: Case management, pattern detection, lethality assessment, intervention planning

view_mode_design.purpose: The TFA website has a public/technical view toggle. Public view shows plain-language content (x_safe_public_* fields) for victims and non-specialists. Technical view shows STIX fields (name, description, kill_chain_phases, etc.) for researchers and practitioners.
view_mode_design.how_it_works: The public content fields (x_safe_public_title, x_safe_public_summary, x_safe_public_safety_warning, x_safe_public_notices, x_safe_public_actions) drive the public view. The standard STIX fields (name, description) drive the technical view. x_safe_view_mode controls which views a technique appears in.

field_mapping_public_view.Technique title: x_safe_public_title (falls back to name if null)
field_mapping_public_view.Technique description: x_safe_public_summary (falls back to description if null)

field_mapping_technical_view.Mitigations: linked via 'mitigates' relationships to course-of-action objects
field_mapping_technical_view.Detections: linked via 'indicates' relationships to indicator objects

view_mode_design.tfa_website_implementation: The view toggle on the TFA site (gh-pages) is implemented in theme/scripts/view-toggle.js and reads these fields from the STIX bundle. The site defaults to public view.
view_mode_design.backward_compatibility: The existing TFA bundle uses x_tfa_public_* fields. The SAFE extension uses x_safe_public_* fields. When the TFA site is rebuilt to read from the SAFE bundle, it needs to check x_safe_public_* (not x_tfa_public_*). The x_tfa_public_* fields on the existing 74 techniques can be migrated to x_safe_public_* as part of the TFA→SAFE alignment work.

site_architecture.principle: Minimal HTML templates, all varying data from STIX. The STIX bundle is the single source of truth for all content that varies between pages.

technique_pages.technical_view: name, description, kill_chain_phases, x_safe_mode/mechanism/domain, x_safe_detection_difficulty, x_safe_prevalence, x_safe_platforms, x_safe_evidence_types + linked course-of-action (mitigations) and indicator (detections) via relationships

tactic_coordinate_pages.technique_list: Derived from techniques whose kill_chain_phases reference this tactic's x_mitre_shortname

matrix_page.cells: Derived from techniques, grouped by kill_chain_phases. data-public-title from x_safe_public_title. data-tech-title from name.

data_from_site_config.note: These elements are sitewide and do NOT vary per technique or tactic. They belong in a site configuration file (e.g., site-config.json), not in STIX.
data_from_site_config.quick_exit: Exit button URL (currently doodles.google), escape key handler. Sitewide.
data_from_site_config.safety_banner: Browser safety banner shown on first visit. Sitewide.
data_from_site_config.disclaimer: General limitations disclaimer shown on all technique pages. Sitewide.
data_from_site_config.legal_pages: about, licensing, limitations, online-safety, privacy, terms. Static content, not STIX.

ideal_template_count.technique_page: 1 template — reads from STIX attack-pattern object + linked mitigations/indicators
ideal_template_count.tactic_page: 1 template — reads from STIX x-mitre-tactic object + lists techniques under it
ideal_template_count.matrix_page: 1 template — reads from x-mitre-matrix + all tactics + all techniques
ideal_template_count.total: 3 dynamic templates + 5-6 static pages. Everything else is data.

site_architecture.migration_path: Currently each technique has a baked HTML file (74 files). To move to template-driven: (1) ensure all public content is in the STIX bundle (it is), (2) build a static site generator or client-side JS that reads the bundle and populates templates, (3) replace 74 technique HTML files with 1 template. The 12 Python injection scripts on gh-pages would be replaced by the template engine.

objects._comment: === EXTENSION DEFINITION — Declares ALL x_safe_* custom properties ===
objects.name: SAFE Framework Technique Extension
objects.description: Extension properties for the SAFE Framework interpersonal harm technique library. SAFE uses 'coordinates' (mode × mechanism × domain intersections) rather than traditional tactics. This extension covers all vectors: direct, proxy, and tech-facilitated.

x_safe_mode.description: Primary mode of harm — the 'why' of the behaviour

x_safe_mechanism.description: Mechanism of harm — the 'how' the behaviour is enacted

x_safe_domain.description: Domain of impact — 'where' the harm lands

x_safe_vector.description: Harm delivery vector — the pathway between perpetrator and victim

x_safe_is_subtechnique.description: Whether this is a sub-technique of a parent technique

x_safe_parent_technique_id.description: Parent technique ID if sub-technique, null otherwise

x_safe_sexual.description: Whether this technique involves sexual harm

x_safe_detection_difficulty.description: How difficult this technique is to detect or recognise

x_safe_prevalence.description: How commonly this technique is observed

x_safe_evidence_types.description: Types of forensic/documentary evidence that may be available

x_safe_recognition_signals.description: Observable signals in plain language — what someone might notice

x_safe_safety_guidance.description: Safety-critical guidance. What to consider before acting.

x_safe_validation.description: Aggregate validation evidence. No individual case details — only source categories and observation counts. Only populated when meaningful data exists.

status.description: unvalidated = theoretical/literature only. preliminary = limited observations. validated = confirmed across multiple sources. strongly_validated = extensive evidence base.

source_categories.description: Categories of sources that have confirmed this technique exists. No identifying details.

observation_count.description: Approximate number of confirmed observations across all sources. Null if not yet tracked. Only publish when meaningful.

confidence.description: Overall confidence in the technique's validity based on source diversity and observation count.

last_validated.description: ISO 8601 datetime of last validation review. Null if never formally validated.

x_safe_migrated_from.description: Original TFA technique ID if migrated from TFA Matrix, null otherwise

x_safe_platforms.description: Technology platforms (primarily for tech_facilitated vector techniques)

x_safe_public_title.description: Plain-language name for the technique, written for victims and non-specialists. Drives the 'public view' on the TFA website. E.g., 'Someone is tracking my location' rather than 'Stalkerware Installation'.

x_safe_public_summary.description: Accessible description of the technique in plain language. No jargon, no technical detail. Written as if explaining to someone experiencing it. Drives the 'public view' on the TFA website.

x_safe_public_safety_warning.description: Safety-critical warning shown prominently on the public view. E.g., 'If you think monitoring software is on your phone, do not remove it — the person monitoring you may be alerted.' Null if no specific safety warning needed.

x_safe_public_notices.description: Array of observable signals in plain language — 'What You Might Notice.' Each item has a signal (short heading) and detail (explanation). Drives the public view.

signal.description: Short heading, e.g., 'Your phone battery drains much faster than usual'

detail.description: Explanation of why this might indicate this technique

x_safe_public_actions.description: Array of recommended actions in plain language — 'What You Can Do.' Each item has an action (what to do), detail (how), and optional safety_note (caution). Drives the public view.

action.description: Short action heading, e.g., 'Get your device checked'

x_safe_view_mode.description: Controls which view(s) this content is available in. 'both' = shown in public and technical views (default). 'public_only' = shown only in public view. 'technical_only' = shown only in technical view. This allows techniques that are too sensitive or confusing for public display to be hidden from the public view while remaining in the STIX bundle for researchers and platforms.

_tactic_public_fields_note.purpose: Tactic/coordinate objects (x-mitre-tactic) also carry public content fields. These are TOP-LEVEL custom properties on the tactic object (not inside the extensions block) because x-mitre-tactic is already a custom STIX type that supports arbitrary properties.

fields.x_safe_public_name: Plain-language name for the coordinate. E.g., 'Watching & Tracking' instead of 'Surveillance & Tracking'. Null if no public-friendly alternative needed.
fields.x_safe_public_intro: Accessible description of what this coordinate covers. Written for victims and non-specialists.
fields.x_safe_public_safety: Coordinate-level safety warning. Shown at the top of the tactic/coordinate page in public view.

objects.name: SAFE Interpersonal Harm Matrix
objects.description: The SAFE Framework Matrix for interpersonal harm. 27 coordinates (mode × mechanism × domain) across direct, proxy, and tech-facilitated vectors.
tactic_refs: _comment: 27 tactic/coordinate IDs in display order — see coordinate naming table

objects._comment: === COORDINATE (x-mitre-tactic) — SAFE calls these 'coordinates' not 'tactics'. Each represents one intersection of mode × mechanism × domain. The STIX type is x-mitre-tactic for ecosystem compatibility. See coordinate naming table for all 27. ===
objects._naming_approach: Option C: Human-friendly name with category grouping. The name is what people see. The shortname is the machine key. The grouping (Abuse > Force > ...) provides structural context.
objects.name: Physical Violence
objects.description: Direct or threatened physical harm through force. Techniques include hitting, restraint, strangulation, destruction of property near the victim, weapon intimidation, and other actions where force is applied to cause or threaten bodily harm.
objects.x_safe_public_intro: These are ways someone might use direct physical force or the threat of force to cause harm. This includes hitting, restraint, destruction of property, and using weapons to intimidate.
objects.x_safe_public_safety: If you are in immediate danger, contact 000. If you have injuries, seek medical help. You can contact 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) for specialist support 24/7.
objects._comment_public_fields: Tactic/coordinate public content. Same pattern as technique x_safe_public_* fields — drives the public view on the website. These sit at the top level (not in extensions) because x-mitre-tactic is already a custom STIX type.

objects.name: Direct Physical Violence
objects.description: Direct application of physical force by the perpetrator against the victim's body, causing or threatening bodily harm. The perpetrator is the immediate agent — no technological intermediary, no third-party proxy.

x_safe_recognition_signals: Defensive injuries on forearms and hands
extension-definition--acf2f380-0000-4000.x_safe_safety_guidance: Immediate physical safety assessment required. If injuries present, document with consent. Assess lethality indicators (strangulation history, weapon access, escalation pattern). Safety planning should account for escalation risk when perpetrator discovers disclosure.

objects._comment_kill_chains: Direct vector technique: SAFE coordinate + lifecycle phases. No TFA tactic because this is not tech-facilitated.

objects.name: Stalkerware Installation
objects.description: Installing hidden monitoring software on victim's device to track location, messages, calls, photos, and keystrokes.

x_safe_recognition_signals: Phone battery draining much faster than usual
Using more mobile data than expected
Phone feels warm even when not in use
The other person seems to know things they shouldn't
Unfamiliar apps or settings on device
extension-definition--acf2f380-0000-4000.x_safe_safety_guidance: If stalkerware is suspected, do not remove it immediately — the monitoring party may be alerted and could escalate. Get advice from a specialist service first. Consider using a separate safe device for sensitive communications.

x_safe_validation._example_only: This shows what a populated validation field looks like. Only populate when real data exists.

extension-definition--acf2f380-0000-4000.x_safe_public_title: Someone may have put tracking software on my phone
extension-definition--acf2f380-0000-4000.x_safe_public_summary: Hidden apps can be installed on your phone that let someone else see your messages, calls, photos, location, and everything you do on your device. These apps are designed to be invisible — you might not know they're there.
extension-definition--acf2f380-0000-4000.x_safe_public_safety_warning: If you think monitoring software is on your phone, do not remove it yet. The person monitoring you may be alerted when the software is removed, which could put you at risk. Get advice from a specialist service first. Consider using a separate safe device for sensitive communications.

x_safe_public_notices.signal: Your phone battery drains much faster than usual
x_safe_public_notices.detail: Monitoring software runs constantly in the background, using battery power to record and transmit your activity.

x_safe_public_notices.signal: Your phone uses more data than expected
x_safe_public_notices.detail: The software sends copies of your messages, photos, and location to the person monitoring you, using your mobile data.

x_safe_public_notices.signal: Your phone feels warm even when you're not using it
x_safe_public_notices.detail: The monitoring software is always running, which can cause your phone to heat up.

x_safe_public_notices.signal: Someone seems to know things they shouldn't
x_safe_public_notices.detail: If someone knows the content of private conversations, where you've been, or who you've been talking to without you telling them, monitoring software may be how.

x_safe_public_notices.signal: You notice unfamiliar apps or changed settings
x_safe_public_notices.detail: Some monitoring software appears as an app with a generic name, or changes settings like 'install from unknown sources' on Android.

x_safe_public_actions.action: Use a safe device for sensitive communications
x_safe_public_actions.detail: If you suspect your phone is monitored, use a different device (a friend's phone, a library computer) for anything you don't want the other person to see.
x_safe_public_actions.safety_note: Don't suddenly change your behaviour on the monitored phone — this may alert the person.

x_safe_public_actions.action: Contact a specialist service for advice
x_safe_public_actions.detail: Call 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the eSafety Commissioner (esafety.gov.au) for guidance specific to your situation.
x_safe_public_actions.safety_note: Use a safe device to make this call.

x_safe_public_actions.action: Get your device checked by a professional
x_safe_public_actions.detail: Some domestic violence services have tech safety programs that can scan your device. The eSafety Commissioner can also provide guidance.
x_safe_public_actions.safety_note: Do not attempt to remove the software yourself without safety advice first.

objects._comment_kill_chains: Tech-facilitated technique: ALL THREE kill chains. (1) SAFE coordinate for analytical classification. (2) TFA tactic for the public website. (3) Lifecycle phases - appears in preparation (purchase), taking-action (install), and keeping-a-hold (ongoing monitoring). Note multiple lifecycle entries - this is by design.

objects.name: Striking
objects.description: Hitting, slapping, punching, backhanding, or striking with objects. May target face/head or body.

objects._comment: === TECHNIQUE (grooming, new TFA-TA-0008) — Shows the grooming tactic with lifecycle phases spanning the trust-building sequence. ===
objects.name: Boundary Testing & Desensitisation
objects.description: Making incrementally escalating requests to test compliance and normalise boundary violations. Starts small (share location, send a photo) and escalates (send intimate content, meet in person, transfer money). The request-demand-threaten-force escalation sequence.
objects._comment_kill_chains: Grooming technique: SAFE coordinate + TFA tactic + lifecycle. Note lifecycle spans testing-boundaries AND taking-action because boundary testing IS the action in grooming contexts.

x_safe_recognition_signals: Requests start small and gradually get bigger
Making you feel you 'owe' them something
Framing boundary violations as proof of trust or love
extension-definition--acf2f380-0000-4000.x_safe_safety_guidance: Critical detection point — this is where the shift from 'normal relationship' to exploitation becomes visible. If someone is escalating requests and reacting badly to 'no', that is a pattern, not a one-off.
extension-definition--acf2f380-0000-4000.x_safe_public_title: Someone is pushing your boundaries and it keeps getting worse
extension-definition--acf2f380-0000-4000.x_safe_public_summary: This person started with small requests — share your location, let me see your phone, send a photo. Over time the requests got bigger, more personal, more uncomfortable. When you say no, they react badly. This pattern of testing what they can get you to do is not normal relationship behaviour.

x_safe_public_notices.signal: Requests start small and gradually get bigger
x_safe_public_notices.detail: They might start by asking you to share your location 'so they know you're safe,' then escalate to wanting access to your messages, then your passwords.

x_safe_public_notices.signal: They guilt-trip you when you say no
x_safe_public_notices.detail: 'If you loved me you would...' or 'I thought you trusted me.' Making you feel bad for having boundaries.

x_safe_public_notices.signal: They frame boundary violations as proof of love
x_safe_public_notices.detail: 'I only check your phone because I care.' Normal relationships don't require giving up your privacy.

x_safe_public_notices.signal: You feel like you 'owe' them something
x_safe_public_notices.detail: Especially after they've given you gifts, attention, or support — this creates a sense of obligation that they exploit.

x_safe_public_notices.signal: Things that felt uncomfortable now feel normal
x_safe_public_notices.detail: You've gradually adjusted to behaviour that would have alarmed you at the start. This is desensitisation — and it's deliberate.

x_safe_public_actions.detail: If something feels wrong, it probably is. You don't need to justify saying no.
A friend, family member, counsellor, or helpline. Describe the pattern, not just individual incidents.
x_safe_public_actions.safety_note: Use a safe device if you think your communications are monitored.

x_safe_public_actions.action: Know that this is a pattern, not a one-off
x_safe_public_actions.detail: If requests keep escalating and 'no' is never accepted, this is a control pattern. It's not about this one request — it's about establishing that your boundaries don't matter.

objects._comment: === TECHNIQUE (discovery, new TFA-TA-0009) — Prevention-focused. How perpetrators learn techniques. ===
objects.name: Stalkerware Marketing Discovery
objects.description: Encountering commercial stalkerware products through advertising, search results, or app store listings. Products marketed as 'parental monitoring' or 'employee tracking' normalise surveillance and provide accessible tools for intimate partner abuse.
objects._comment_kill_chains: Discovery/preparation technique: pre-attack phase. Lifecycle phases are gathering-information and preparation only. This technique describes HOW someone learns to do harm, not the harm itself.

extension-definition--acf2f380-0000-4000.x_safe_safety_guidance: Prevention-focused technique. This is about the perpetrator's journey, not the victim's experience. Intervention points: app store policy enforcement, advertising platform restrictions, search engine result filtering, public education about what stalkerware actually is.

objects.name: Anti-Stalkerware Scanning
objects.description: Deploy anti-stalkerware detection tools to identify monitoring applications. Scan for apps with excessive permissions including location, microphone, camera, and message access.

objects._pattern_design_note: Behavioural indicators don't map cleanly to standard STIX SCOs (which are designed for network traffic, file hashes, etc.). Current approach: minimal valid pattern as placeholder, with the indicator's value carried in name, description, and relationships. This is an acknowledged design limitation shared by other behavioural frameworks. The indicator is still useful to platforms — they ingest the object, display its name/description, and traverse its relationships to linked techniques.
objects.name: Anomalous Battery Consumption
objects.description: Device battery depletes significantly faster than baseline, potentially indicating continuous background data transmission by monitoring software.

objects._comment: === NOTE — Legal/legislative context linked to techniques. Standard STIX type, every platform understands it. Use for jurisdiction-specific legislation, case law references, or policy context without identifying individual cases. ===
objects.content: In Australia, installing monitoring software without consent may constitute surveillance device offences under state/territory legislation (e.g., Surveillance Devices Act 2004 (Cth), Surveillance Devices Act 1999 (Vic)). Stalkerware installation may also constitute a family violence offence where a family violence intervention order is in place. The eSafety Commissioner has powers to investigate technology-facilitated abuse under the Online Safety Act 2021.

objects.description: Anomalous Battery Consumption may indicate Stalkerware Installation.

_coordinate_naming_table._approach: Option C — Human-friendly names with structural grouping. The name is what people see. The shortname (x_mitre_shortname) is the machine key that techniques reference via kill_chain_phases.phase_name. Grouped by mode for display. External IDs use SAFE-C- prefix (C for coordinate). THESE ARE DRAFT PROPOSALS requiring Em's review.
_coordinate_naming_table._format: coordinate → { name (human-friendly), description (one line), external_id (for STIX refs) }
_coordinate_naming_table._grouping_note: Display could group by mode (Abuse | Exploitation | Neglect) as top-level tabs or colour bands, with mechanism × domain as the visible grid within each.

abuse.force.psychological.name: Threats & Intimidation

abuse.force.environmental.name: Property & Resource Destruction
abuse.force.environmental.description: Using force to damage, destroy, or control the victim's physical environment, belongings, or resources.

abuse.manipulation.physical.name: Physical Manipulation
abuse.manipulation.physical.description: Using deception, coercion, or exploitation of trust to control the victim's body or physical autonomy.

abuse.manipulation.psychological.name: Psychological Manipulation
abuse.manipulation.psychological.description: Using deception, gaslighting, or emotional exploitation to distort the victim's reality, self-perception, or decision-making.

abuse.manipulation.environmental.name: Environmental Manipulation
abuse.manipulation.environmental.description: Using deception or exploitation of systems to control the victim's living situation, finances, or access to resources.

abuse.isolation.physical.name: Physical Confinement
abuse.isolation.physical.description: Restricting the victim's physical movement, access to people, or ability to leave.

abuse.isolation.psychological.name: Psychological Isolation
abuse.isolation.psychological.description: Cutting the victim off from emotional support, undermining their relationships, or creating dependence.

abuse.isolation.environmental.name: Environmental Isolation
abuse.isolation.environmental.description: Controlling the victim's access to external resources, services, transport, or community.

exploitation.force.physical.name: Forced Physical Exploitation
exploitation.force.physical.description: Using force to exploit the victim's body for the perpetrator's benefit — labour, physical servitude.

exploitation.force.psychological.name: Forced Psychological Exploitation
exploitation.force.psychological.description: Using force or coercion to exploit the victim's emotional labour, compliance, or mental capacity.

exploitation.force.environmental.name: Forced Resource Exploitation
exploitation.force.environmental.description: Using force to exploit the victim's financial resources, property, or economic output.

exploitation.manipulation.physical.name: Manipulative Physical Exploitation

exploitation.manipulation.psychological.name: Manipulative Psychological Exploitation
exploitation.manipulation.psychological.description: Using deception to exploit the victim's emotions, trust, or cognitive vulnerabilities for the perpetrator's gain.

exploitation.manipulation.environmental.name: Manipulative Resource Exploitation
exploitation.manipulation.environmental.description: Using deception or manipulation to exploit the victim's finances, property, or legal standing.

exploitation.isolation.physical.name: Exploitative Physical Isolation

exploitation.isolation.psychological.name: Exploitative Psychological Isolation
exploitation.isolation.psychological.description: Isolating the victim psychologically to enable ongoing exploitation — creating dependence to maintain access.

exploitation.isolation.environmental.name: Exploitative Environmental Isolation
exploitation.isolation.environmental.description: Controlling the victim's environment to enable ongoing exploitation — trapping them in exploitative living or work conditions.

neglect.force.psychological.name: Enforced Emotional Deprivation
neglect.force.psychological.description: Deliberately withholding emotional care, acknowledgment, or psychological support.

neglect.force.environmental.name: Enforced Resource Deprivation

neglect.manipulation.physical.name: Manipulative Physical Neglect
neglect.manipulation.physical.description: Using deception or manipulation to avoid responsibility for the victim's physical care or safety.

neglect.manipulation.psychological.name: Manipulative Emotional Neglect
neglect.manipulation.psychological.description: Using manipulation to avoid emotional responsibility — making the victim feel their needs are unreasonable.

neglect.manipulation.environmental.name: Manipulative Resource Neglect
neglect.manipulation.environmental.description: Using manipulation to avoid providing resources while maintaining the appearance of care.

neglect.isolation.physical.name: Isolative Physical Neglect

neglect.isolation.psychological.name: Isolative Emotional Neglect
neglect.isolation.psychological.description: Withholding emotional support while isolating the victim from alternative sources of care.

neglect.isolation.environmental.name: Isolative Resource Neglect
neglect.isolation.environmental.description: Withholding environmental resources while cutting the victim off from alternative access.
